title: Is Harvey vs. Legora Turning into Harvey vs. Legora vs. Claude?
author: Zach Abramowitz

dom.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: Abramowitz accepts the competitive-workflow shift and materially strengthens it with a concrete example of Quinn Emanuel bypassing application-layer vendors to build legal workflows directly on Claude. He also frames major productivity gains and displacement of Harvey and Legora as conditional possibilities rather than established outcomes, consistent with the synthesis’s caution.
qs: We are already seeing top-tier litigators bypass off-the-shelf products to build directly on base models.
If litigators can achieve an order-of-magnitude productivity gain just by directly prompting Claude as a thought partner, what does that mean for companies like Harvey and Legora?

kp.k: Claude may challenge legal application-layer vendors
kp.d: Abramowitz frames direct use of Anthropic’s Claude as a possible competitive threat to legal-AI products such as Harvey and Legora. This is presented as an open market question rather than an evidenced finding or definite prediction.
qs: Is Claude stealing all of Harvey and Legora's attention?
We went deep on whether Claude is going to steal Harvey and Legora's lunch.
If litigators can achieve an order-of-magnitude productivity gain just by directly prompting Claude as a thought partner, what does that mean for companies like Harvey and Legora?

kp.k: Litigators are building directly on base models
kp.d: The author reports that some top-tier litigators are bypassing off-the-shelf legal-AI products and building proprietary systems directly on foundation models. Quinn Emanuel is the sole example provided, so the document does not establish how widespread this practice is.
qs: We are already seeing top-tier litigators bypass off-the-shelf products to build directly on base models.
For example, Quinn Emanuel built their own proprietary system (the "Kerch Bench") entirely on top of Claude.

Instead of relying on an application-layer company, they are structuring their own case data, distilling depositions, and building custom Claude "skills" to draft briefs and conduct early case assessments.

kp.k: Direct Claude use could transform litigation tasks
kp.d: The Quinn Emanuel example identifies case-data structuring, deposition distillation, brief drafting and early case assessment as litigation workflows being configured around Claude. The claimed possibility of an order-of-magnitude productivity gain is expressly conditional and is not supported here by benchmark results, measured outcomes or a stated timeframe.

kp.k: Elite firms are partnering with multiple model providers
kp.d: Abramowitz reports that Freshfields announced a Google partnership and then an Anthropic partnership. The document treats these announcements as relevant to legal-AI competition but provides no details about deployment scope, contractual terms, adoption, performance or effects on lawyers’ work.
qs: We also unpacked Freshfields' announcement that they're partnering with Google, followed by their announcement that they're partnering with Anthropic.

kp.k: Claude is framed for firms and departments
kp.d: The source states that Claude’s legal-workflow use is relevant both to law firms and to in-house legal departments. It does not describe specific in-house tasks, evidence of adoption or differences between provider-side and buyer-side use.
qs: We talked about why someone would use Claude for legal workflows, both if they're in a law firm or an in-house legal department.

kp.k: Author argues hallucination concerns are overstated
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that lawyers give AI hallucinations disproportionate weight because human lawyers and judges also make errors involving facts or law. He presents appellate review as a correction mechanism for human error, but supplies no comparative error rates, studies or court data establishing equivalence between human mistakes and generative-AI hallucinations.
qs: And finally, we discussed why lawyers are blowing AI hallucinations out of proportion.
As we've discussed before on this show, human lawyers and judges hallucinate all the time.
In fact, the entire appellate court system is predicated on the fact that humans make errors and hallucinate facts or law, which is exactly why we need a system to correct them.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Abramowitz claims that some top-tier litigators are already bypassing packaged legal-AI products to build custom workflows directly on foundation models.
pts.d: He presents Quinn Emanuel's proprietary Claude-based system as an example, covering case-data structuring, deposition distillation, brief drafting and early case assessment. He raises competitive displacement of Harvey and Legora as a question rather than an established outcome. Likewise, the order-of-magnitude productivity gain is posed conditionally, not reported as a measured result. Separately, Abramowitz argues that lawyers exaggerate AI hallucination concerns, drawing an analogy to errors made by human lawyers and judges. This is his argument, not a reported comparative error-rate finding; the passage does not provide a distinct claim attributable to Richard Tromans.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers named examples and an analogy, but no quantitative productivity or reliability evidence.
pts.d: The reported Quinn Emanuel implementation is the concrete example supporting direct foundation-model use. Freshfields' announced partnerships with Google and Anthropic provide additional context for law-firm engagement with foundation-model providers, but the source does not state that Freshfields has replaced application-layer products. No benchmark, study, methodology or measured productivity result supports the conditional order-of-magnitude gain. The hallucination argument relies on the author's assertion that humans also err and on the appellate system as an error-correction analogy; it supplies no measured model error rates or court sanctions incidents.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Direct model adoption is described as already occurring in the source's 2026 context; future competitive effects remain conditional and undated.
pts.d: The source includes an April 17, 2026 post and describes direct model building as a current development. Its competitive question depends on litigators being able to obtain large productivity gains by prompting Claude as a thought partner. The concrete implementation also involves firm-specific data structuring and custom skills. There is no deadline, adoption forecast or definite prediction that Harvey or Legora will lose business. The hallucination argument concerns present attitudes rather than a forecast of improving model reliability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are sophisticated litigation firms, legal-AI application vendors and foundation-model providers; in-house departments are also mentioned as potential users.
pts.d: Top-tier litigators are portrayed as gaining the ability to develop tailored litigation workflows rather than depending on packaged applications. Harvey and Legora are the legal-tech vendors whose competitive position is questioned, while Claude/Anthropic is presented as a direct platform for legal work. Freshfields illustrates large-firm partnerships with model providers. Law firms and in-house legal departments are both identified as settings for Claude workflows, but specific in-house outcomes are not supplied. The 'thought partner' framing describes lawyer augmentation, not autonomous replacement. The source does not specify effects on staffing, fees, client outcomes or access to justice.
